name: AI-Driven Reproducibility Crisis
description: The integration of AI in scientific research is exacerbating a structural reproducibility crisis—not merely as a technical glitch but as a systemic issue rooted in opacity, non-determinism, and fragmented tooling.

name: Technical Transparency Deficit
description: AI systems (especially LLMs and deep learning pipelines) frequently lack documentation of model versions, training data provenance, hyperparameter configurations, and stochastic seeds—making independent replication of computational experiments nearly impossible.

name: Black-Box Automation
description: Use of opaque AI tools for data cleaning, statistical inference, or hypothesis generation without exposing intermediate logic or decision thresholds—undermining traceability and auditability.

name: Non-Deterministic Outputs
description: Stochastic elements in AI training/inference (e.g., random weight initialization, dropout, sampling-based generation) produce irreproducible outputs even with identical inputs and code, violating core reproducibility norms.

name: Fragmented Tooling Ecosystem
description: Proliferation of incompatible, poorly versioned AI libraries (e.g., PyTorch vs. JAX variants), container environments, and cloud-specific runtimes creates environment-dependent results that hinder cross-platform replication.

name: AI-Augmented Research Practices
description: Growing adoption of AI for literature synthesis, experimental design suggestion, code generation, and manuscript drafting—often without methodological validation or transparency about AI’s role in the research chain.

name: Reproducibility-as-Transparency Principle
description: Reproducibility in AI-augmented science depends less on exact bit-for-bit replication and more on full transparency of data, code, models, metadata, and human-AI interaction protocols.

name: Standardized AI Provenance Frameworks
description: Emerging proposals (e.g., MLflow + CodeOcean integrations, AI Model Cards, Data Statements) to mandate structured reporting of AI components used in publications—including model cards, dataset licenses, and inference-time randomness logging.

name: AI Reproducibility Paradox
description: Tension between AI’s promise to *enhance* reproducibility (via automation, error reduction, meta-analysis) and its observed role in *eroding* it (via opacity, complexity, and unvalidated automation).

name: AI-Driven Automation of Reproducibility Checks
description: Use of AI tools (e.g., code linters, data provenance tracers, statistical re-execution bots) to automatically verify computational reproducibility across publications and repositories.

name: Open science practices
description: Norms and infrastructures promoting transparency and accessibility in research, including open data, open code, pre-registration, and open peer review.

name: Algorithmic Opacity in Research Pipelines
description: AI models embedded in scientific workflows (e.g., preprocessing, feature selection, anomaly detection) often lack transparency, hindering independent verification of analytical steps.

name: Reproducibility Crisis Amplification
description: Widespread, uncritical adoption of AI in research—without standardized documentation or validation—exacerbates the existing reproducibility crisis, particularly in data-intensive fields.

name: Staged Maturation of AI Tools
description: AI’s impact on reproducibility evolves across temporal stages: initial disruption (increased opacity), intermediate stabilization (emergence of audit-ready tools), and mature integration (embedded reproducibility-by-design).

name: Structural Governance Deficits
description: Lack of field-wide standards, incentives, or infrastructure for auditing AI-augmented methods—e.g., no mandatory model cards, versioned training data logs, or executable workflow metadata.

name: AI-Augmented Documentation
description: AI systems that auto-generate human-readable method summaries, dependency graphs, or counterfactual sensitivity reports to enhance transparency and replicability.

name: Ambivalent Impact of AI on Reproducibility
description: AI simultaneously enhances and undermines reproducibility: it enables scalable validation *and* introduces novel sources of irreproducibility through black-box automation and stochastic outputs.

name: Reproducibility-by-Design Paradigm
description: A proposed governance framework requiring AI-integrated research to embed reproducibility features from inception—e.g., containerized environments, traceable data lineage, and deterministic seeding protocols.

name: AI-enhanced reproducibility
description: AI tools (e.g., automated code generation, data cleaning, statistical validation) can improve research reproducibility by reducing human error and standardizing analytical workflows.

name: Disciplinary asymmetry
description: The impact of AI on reproducibility varies significantly across disciplines—strongest in computational fields (e.g., bioinformatics, NLP), weakest in qualitative or theory-heavy domains (e.g., anthropology, philosophy) due to differences in data structure, methodological norms, and tool adoption.

name: Structural failure in evidence base
description: A critical portion of empirical AI-assisted studies lacks transparent documentation of model versions, hyperparameters, seed values, or training data provenance—undermining independent replication despite apparent methodological rigor.

name: Black-box automation risk
description: Widespread use of opaque AI tools (e.g., LLM-based analysis assistants, autoML pipelines) introduces untraceable decision points that obscure analytical reasoning and violate core reproducibility principles like transparency and auditability.

name: LLM Provider Failures
description: Failures in Large Language Model (LLM) providers, which can lead to significant disruptions and security issues.

name: Reproducibility paradox
description: AI simultaneously increases *technical* reproducibility (via automation) while decreasing *epistemic* reproducibility (via reduced interpretability and accountability), creating a tension where outputs are replicable but not understandable or justifiable.

name: Calibrated impact assessment
description: A multidimensional evaluation framework that quantifies AI’s net effect on reproducibility by weighting gains (e.g., speed, consistency) against losses (e.g., opacity, dependency drift) across technical, procedural, and sociological dimensions.

name: AI documentation deficit
description: Less than 12% of AI-augmented papers in high-impact journals report full computational provenance (code, environment, model cards), constituting a systemic gap in reproducibility infrastructure.

name: Tool dependency drift
description: Rapid evolution of AI libraries and APIs causes version incompatibility over time, making previously reproducible workflows non-functional without active maintenance—a growing source of 'bit rot' in computational science.

name: AI-assisted research
description: Use of artificial intelligence tools (e.g., LLMs, automated data analysis, code generation) in scientific workflows including hypothesis generation, experiment design, data processing, and manuscript writing.

name: Research reproducibility
description: The ability of independent researchers to obtain consistent results using the same methods, data, and computational environment as the original study.

name: AI-induced opacity

name: Automatisation des tâches expérimentales
description: Utilisation de l'IA pour automatiser les tâches répétitives et complexes dans les expériences, ce qui peut réduire les variations dues aux erreurs humaines.

name: Standardisation des protocoles expérimentaux
description: Utilisation de l'IA pour standardiser les protocoles expérimentaux, ce qui peut augmenter la cohérence et la reproductibilité des résultats.

name: Analyse de données par l'IA
description: Utilisation de l'IA pour analyser de grandes quantités de données, ce qui peut aider à identifier des tendances et des modèles plus précis.

name: Réduction des erreurs humaines
description: L'utilisation de l'IA peut réduire les erreurs dues à la variabilité humaine, contribuant ainsi à une meilleure reproductibilité des expériences.

name: Controverse sur la transparence des algorithmes d'IA
description: La complexité et l'opacité des algorithmes d'IA peuvent poser des défis pour la transparence et la vérification des méthodes utilisées, affectant potentiellement la reproductibilité.

name: International Response
description: The response from the international community, including aid and diplomatic efforts, to address the crisis.

name: Mixed Economic Effects
description: Varied impacts on different sectors and aspects of the economy, including both positive and negative outcomes.

name: Nuclear Safety and Security
description: Policies and measures aimed at ensuring the safe and secure operation of nuclear facilities to prevent accidents and malicious acts.

name: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
description: A branch of computer science that aims to create software or machines that exhibit human-like intelligence.

name: Reproducibility in Scientific Research
description: The ability to replicate the results of a scientific study using the same methods and data.

name: AI-Enhanced Data Analysis
description: The use of AI to process, analyze, and interpret large datasets more efficiently and accurately.

name: Automation of Experimental Procedures
description: The use of AI to automate and standardize experimental procedures, reducing human error and variability.

name: Increased Reproducibility
description: AI can enhance the reproducibility of scientific research by automating and standardizing processes.

name: Data Bias and Quality Issues
description: AI systems can inadvertently perpetuate or amplify biases present in the training data, leading to skewed results.

name: Transparency and Explainability
description: There is a growing trend towards developing more transparent and explainable AI models to ensure trust and reliability in scientific research.

name: Geopolitical Implications
description: The broader international and regional political consequences that may arise from the attack on the Iranian power plant.

name: UN Nuclear Agency
description: The United Nations body responsible for overseeing the peaceful use of nuclear energy and technology, commonly known as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

name: Iran Power Plant Attack
description: A reported cyber-physical attack on a power plant in Iran, which has raised concerns about the security and safety of nuclear infrastructure.

name: Regulatory Burden on Innovation
description: Argument that stringent AI regulations impose compliance costs and administrative burdens that stifle innovation and reduce competitiveness.

name: Défis de l'IA pour la reproductibilité
description: L'utilisation de l'IA peut aussi introduire des défis, comme la complexité des modèles, la dépendance à des données spécifiques et la difficulté de comprendre les processus de décision.

name: Opportunités de l'IA pour la reproductibilité
description: L'IA peut améliorer la reproductibilité en automatisant certaines tâches, en réduisant les erreurs humaines et en standardisant les protocoles expérimentaux.

name: Intelligence Artificielle (IA)
description: Technologies et systèmes qui simulent l'intelligence humaine pour effectuer des tâches complexes.

name: Nuclear Safety Concerns
description: Issues related to the security and safety of nuclear facilities, which are heightened by the reported attack.

name: Regulatory Trust Advantage
description: Argument that clear AI regulations build consumer trust and create a stable environment that can enhance long-term competitiveness.

name: Reproductibilité de la recherche scientifique
description: Capacité à reproduire les résultats expérimentaux d'une expérience ou d'une analyse par une autre équipe de recherche.

name: Automatisation des expériences
description: Utilisation de l'IA pour automatiser les processus expérimentaux, réduisant ainsi les erreurs humaines et augmentant la cohérence.

name: Biais algorithmiques
description: Les biais présents dans les données d'entraînement de l'IA peuvent se propager et affecter la reproductibilité des résultats.

name: Humanitarian Impact
description: The war has led to significant humanitarian issues, including displacement and suffering of civilians.

name: Economic Impact
description: The war has caused economic disruptions, affecting both Iran and its trading partners.

name: Geopolitical Impact
description: The conflict has altered geopolitical dynamics in the region, with implications for international relations.

name: Geopolitical Challenges
description: Iran faces numerous geopolitical challenges, including regional tensions and international sanctions.

name: Media Narratives
description: The way the media portrays the Iran war, influencing public opinion and policy decisions.

name: Diplomatic Efforts
description: Ongoing diplomatic initiatives aimed at resolving the conflict and reducing tensions.

name: Developmental Impacts
description: The war's effects on Iran's economic and social development, including potential long-term consequences.

name: Iran War
description: The conflict involving Iran, which is the primary focus of the analysis.

name: Geopolitical Tensions
description: Increasing political and military tensions between nations, particularly in the Middle East, exacerbated by the attack.

name: Emission Reductions
description: Decrease in the amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere as a result of policy measures.

name: GDP Effects
description: Impact on the Gross Domestic Product, which is a measure of the economic performance of a country.

name: Carbon Leakage
description: The risk that stringent EU carbon pricing causes energy-intensive industries to relocate production to regions with less rigorous climate regulation, undermining both competitiveness and global emissions reductions.

name: Long-term Economic Benefits
description: Over the long term, a carbon tax can stimulate innovation and investment in clean energy, potentially leading to economic benefits.

name: Reduction in Emissions
description: Implementing a carbon tax can lead to a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions as it incentivizes lower carbon usage.

name: Economic Efficiency
description: A well-designed carbon tax can be an economically efficient way to reduce emissions compared to command-and-control regulations.

name: Revenue Recycling
description: Using the revenue from a carbon tax to reduce other taxes or invest in green technology can mitigate negative economic impacts.

name: Carbon Tax
description: A tax levied on the carbon content of fuels, aimed at reducing carbon dioxide emissions.

name: Economic Growth
description: The increase in the inflation-adjusted market value of the goods and services produced by an economy over time.

name: AI Compliance Costs
description: The financial and operational costs associated with complying with AI regulatory requirements, potentially affecting smaller firms disproportionately.

name: Brussels Effect
description: The phenomenon where EU regulations influence global standards, potentially giving European companies advantages in compliant markets.

name: Impact of Carbon Tax on Economic Growth
description: The effect that implementing a carbon tax has on the overall economic growth of a country or region.

name: Green Innovation and Competitiveness
description: The hypothesis that carbon pricing stimulates investment in clean technologies and process innovation, potentially enhancing long-run industrial competitiveness rather than undermining it.

name: Innovation Fund (EU ETS)
description: An EU funding mechanism financed by auctioning ETS allowances, designed to support demonstration of innovative low-carbon technologies in energy-intensive sectors.

name: Competitiveness–Climate Policy Trade-off
description: The ongoing debate over whether ambitious EU carbon pricing necessarily harms industrial competitiveness or whether complementary policies can reconcile both objectives.

name: Phase-out of Free Allowances
description: The scheduled reduction and eventual elimination of freely allocated ETS allowances for industry between 2026 and 2034, increasing direct carbon costs for affected sectors.

name: Carbon Price Trajectory to 2030
description: The projected increase in EU ETS allowance prices toward and beyond €100/tonne CO2 by 2030, driven by tightening caps and rising demand for allowances.

name: ETS Phase 4 Reform (2021–2030)
description: The fourth trading phase of the EU ETS, featuring a steeper linear reduction factor for the emissions cap and a gradual phase-out of free allowances, increasing cost pressure on industry by 2030.

name: Green Innovation and Low-Carbon Investment
description: Carbon pricing is theorized and empirically observed to stimulate R&D and capital investment in low-carbon technologies, potentially improving long-run competitiveness through first-mover advantages.

name: Porter Hypothesis
description: The theoretical proposition that well-designed environmental regulation can spur innovation and improve long-term competitiveness, used to argue that ETS need not harm industry.

name: Competitiveness Impact of ETS — Negative View
description: The position that rising carbon prices under the ETS impose significant cost burdens on EU industries, eroding profit margins and market share relative to non-EU competitors not subject to equivalent carbon costs.

name: Carbon Cost Pass-Through
description: The degree to which industries transfer ETS compliance costs to product prices; high pass-through can protect profit margins but may reduce demand and market share in price-sensitive global markets.

name: Competitiveness Impact of ETS — Positive View
description: The position that ETS-driven decarbonization investments and innovation create long-term competitive advantages, and that CBAM and free allocations sufficiently mitigate short-term cost disadvantages.

name: ETS Carbon Price Trajectory to 2030
description: EU ETS allowance prices have risen substantially (exceeding €80–100/tonne in recent years) and are projected to remain elevated or increase further toward 2030, amplifying cost pressures on industry.

name: Innovation Fund (EU)
description: An EU funding mechanism financed by ETS allowance revenues, designed to support demonstration of innovative low-carbon technologies in energy-intensive industries, partially offsetting competitiveness impacts.

name: Sectoral Heterogeneity in ETS Impact
description: Empirical evidence that the competitive impact of EU carbon pricing varies significantly across industrial sectors depending on trade exposure, abatement potential, and energy intensity.

name: Abatement Cost
description: The cost incurred by industries to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions through technology upgrades, fuel switching, or process changes, a key determinant of ETS compliance burden.

name: 2030 EU Climate Target
description: The EU's legally binding commitment to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% compared to 1990 levels by 2030, driving the tightening of ETS caps and increasing carbon price pressure on industry.

name: Windfall Profits under ETS
description: Some industries, particularly power generators, have historically earned windfall profits by passing through the cost of free allowances to consumers, raising questions about the efficiency and equity of free allocation.

name: EU Emissions Trading System (ETS)
description: The European Union's cap-and-trade mechanism that sets a price on carbon emissions for industrial sectors, requiring companies to hold allowances for each tonne of CO2 emitted.

name: EU Carbon Pricing
description: The broader framework of pricing carbon emissions within the EU, encompassing ETS allowances and related fiscal instruments designed to internalize the cost of greenhouse gas emissions.

name: Industrial Competitiveness
description: The ability of EU-based industries to compete effectively in domestic and global markets, potentially affected by the additional cost burden imposed by carbon pricing mechanisms.

name: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)
description: An EU policy instrument that imposes a carbon price on imports of certain goods from countries with weaker climate policies, intended to level the playing field and prevent carbon leakage.

name: Free Allowance Allocation
description: The practice under the EU ETS of distributing a portion of emissions allowances to industrial sectors at no cost, historically used to protect competitiveness and reduce carbon leakage risk.

name: ETS Phase 4 Reform
description: The fourth phase of the EU ETS (2021–2030) featuring a steeper linear reduction factor for allowances, accelerating the pace of decarbonization obligations for covered industries.

name: Energy-Intensive Industries (EIIs)
description: Sectors such as steel, cement, chemicals, and aluminium that face disproportionately high compliance costs under carbon pricing due to their large emissions footprints.

name: Competitiveness Impact Assessment
description: Analytical approach used to quantify how carbon pricing policies affect production costs, market share, and investment decisions of EU industries relative to global competitors.

name: Green Industrial Policy
description: EU and member-state strategies combining carbon pricing with subsidies, innovation funding, and regulatory support to maintain industrial competitiveness during the low-carbon transition.

name: Innovation Fund
description: An EU funding mechanism financed by ETS allowance revenues that supports demonstration of innovative low-carbon technologies in energy-intensive industries.

name: Asymmetric Carbon Regulation
description: The contested issue that EU industries face higher carbon costs than competitors in countries without equivalent carbon pricing, creating an uneven global competitive landscape.

name: Decarbonization Investment
description: The accelerating capital expenditure by EU industries in low-carbon technologies (e.g., green hydrogen, electrification) partly driven by rising ETS carbon prices.

name: ETS Windfall Profits
description: Criticism that some industries receiving free allowances have generated excess profits by passing carbon costs to consumers while not bearing full compliance costs.

name: Linear Reduction Factor (LRF)
description: The annual percentage by which the EU ETS cap on total allowances is reduced, set at 4.3% from 2024 onward under Phase 4 reforms to tighten supply and raise carbon prices.

name: Market Stability Reserve (MSR)
description: An EU ETS mechanism that adjusts the supply of allowances in circulation to stabilize carbon prices and prevent excessive volatility.

name: Fit for 55 Package
description: The EU legislative package targeting a 55% reduction in net greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, which includes ETS reforms, CBAM introduction, and sector-specific measures affecting industrial competitiveness.

name: SME Competitiveness Burden
description: Small and medium enterprises in covered sectors face proportionally higher administrative and compliance costs under the ETS compared to large industrial players.
